BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Above average temperatures will remain through the week as an upper-level ridge persists over the Great Basin. Dry conditions, mostly clear skies, and temperatures 10 to 15 degrees above normal are expected through the mid-week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above normal temperatures through the weekend.
- A weak cold front brings a slight chance of showers to Baker County and the west central Idaho mountains on Sunday.
- Significantly above normal temperatures develop next week, peaking Wednesday around 15 degrees above normal with potential record highs.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The upper-level ridge will be overhead through early afternoon, providing mostly clear skies and warm temperatures of 10-15 degrees above normal. The ridge will begin to slowly move east late this afternoon and evening, with a weak shortwave trough and associated cold front tracking across the Pacific Northwest through the weekend. Higher precipitation chances will stay NW of the area, with only a slight chance expected across Baker County and the west central Idaho mountains Sunday. The rest of the area will see breezier winds and increased mid- and high-level cloud cover. Late Monday, a stronger shortwave trough will move through the area. Precipitation chances of 10-30% are forecast for higher elevations Monday night. Snow levels during this period will hover around 7000 ft MSL. Despite the increased cloud cover and the weak frontal passage, temperatures will remain unseasonably above average into next week.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Above average temperatures will remain through the week as an upper-level ridge persists over the Great Basin. Dry conditions, mostly clear skies, and temperatures 10 to 15 degrees above normal are expected through the mid-week. Upper- level troughing in the Gulf of Alaska will remain offshore until late Thursday when the ridge moves east and weakens. Come Friday, models agree on the eastward movement of the strong longwave trough offshore, but not on how far inland. This will be the leading difference in what the weather could be next weekend, with possibilities ranging from widespread precipitation to none at all. For now, Friday and Saturday will see slight chances of rain / mountain snow and the beginning of a slight cooldown.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: At the risk of sounding like a broken record... the next 5 days and likely beyond look warm with above average temperatures, abundant sunshine, and near-zero chances for any precipitation.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above normal temperatures and dry conditions are expected through the entire week ahead.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: There has been almost no precipitation in the high country this afternoon and evening. Additionally, there is practically no chance for precipitation through the rest of the night and beyond for our forecast area. Lows tonight are forecast to be similar to the last few nights with temperatures around freezing for the plains and in the upper teens to 20s for the high country.

At the risk of sounding like a broken record... the next 5 days and likely beyond look warm with above average temperatures, abundant sunshine, and near-zero chances for any precipitation. Current water vapor imagery shows an upper-level ridge starting to build over California and the Great Basin. This ridge will quickly expand to the east on Saturday influencing our weather for the foreseeable future. Highs on Saturday are forecast to top out a bit warmer than Friday with low to mid 60s across the plains. There will be less clouds than Friday given increased subsidence. Sunday and Monday remain on track to be the warmest days of the week with the mid- level ridge peaking in strength for our area. It is even trending a bit stronger in recent model runs. Ensemble guidance remains in good agreement of high temperatures in the upper 60s to approaching 70 for the urban corridor and eastern plains for Sunday and Monday. Even then, for Tuesday through at least Friday, ensemble guidance shows highs for the plains staying in the low to mid 60s. There could be some slight fluctuations in high temperatures during this period depending on if we can get some cold air advection as well as less of an influence from the upper-level ridge. Even then, no significant cooldown is on the horizon through at least the end of next week. A trough looks to pass off to our northeast on Wednesday, but could bring some breezier conditions for the eastern plains. There is still a broad consensus that the ridge should break down by next weekend, which generally looks to bring cooler temperatures and could bring at least some chance for precipitation as we approach the 3rd week of November.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: The long term forecast for the Intermountain West is rather boring to say the least. Upper level ridging will put our region in a subsequent chokehold for the next 7 days. This is great news for anyone that needs to build a house or pour concrete this week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Near to just above average temperatures and dry conditions are expected through this weekend.
- Breezier winds return Sunday into Monday, however fire weather conditions are not anticipated at this time.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Another beautiful day is on deck as we sit firmly under high pressure aloft, bringing partly sunny skies with a few passing high clouds. These high clouds may hamper highs today, keeping them slightly cooler then what could be. Even so, expect high temperatures to top out slightly above average for this time of year. Locations along and west of the Laramie Range will see highs climb into the low 50s while many locations along and east of the I- 25 corridor will see highs soar into the low 60s, possibly approaching the mid 60s across the Nebraska Panhandle. Lows tonight will bottom out into the low 30s as skies clear and radiational cooling takes place, a few colder spots may see lows dip into the upper 20s. Winds will pose no threat as we continue to sit under the influence of high pressure, expect mainly calm winds today for many locations across the CWA. As we head into Sunday, more of the same as the ridge axis aloft sits firmly over our forecast area. This will set the stage for another warm day, warmer then Saturday, with highs topping out in the mid 50s to low 60s along and west of I-25 and low 60s to upper 60s east of the corridor. With a few locations in far eastern Wyoming and in the Nebraska Panhandle having the chance of hitting 70. Another thing regarding Sunday compared to days past, it will be a bit windier, especially in our wind prones. The mid-level flow will ramp up with 700 mb westerly winds increasing into the 35 to 45 knot range. With ample subsidence, negative Omega (GFS), these breezier winds will make it down to the surface, especially along the higher peaks of the Laramie Range. One final note, lows Sunday night will be several degrees warmer then previous nights as lows dive into the mid 30s west of I-25 and upper 30s to low 40s along and east of the I-25 corridor.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The long term forecast for the Intermountain West is rather boring to say the least. Upper level ridging will put our region in a subsequent chokehold for the next 7 days. This is great news for anyone that needs to build a house or pour concrete this week. Sunday, looks to be the warmest day of the week in the long term forecast when the ridge looks like an amplified sine wave that advects in warmer but drier air into the region. High temperatures look to be in the mid 60's for areas east of I-25 with the potential of some areas to reach 70. 700mb temperatures look to peak around 6 or 7C which will also give us slightly warmer temperatures in the upper 30s overnight compared to the upper 20s we had the past several days. During the next work week, there will be multiple low pressure system moving up and over our ridge dragging some colder air with it. While these systems don't seem to currently present our region with precipitation chances. It will knock our high temperatures down to the more seasonable mid 50's to low 60's and overnight lows into the upper 20's to low 30's as 700mb temperatures hover between 0 and 1C.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Models are in good agreement with each other and with satellite imagery showing the cut off low descending over southwestern Arizona into northern Mexico where it will turn to the east Saturday to eject into Texas by Monday before turning to the northeast.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Morning fog is possible in the valleys, especially in the usual places (Uinta Basin, Hayden, Gunnison) and across the southern areas where so much rain fell. Look for any fog to burn off by about 9 AM.
- Expect warm temperatures about five degrees above normal, and drier conditions through the weekend and the coming work week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Models are in good agreement with each other and with satellite imagery showing the cut off low descending over southwestern Arizona into northern Mexico where it will turn to the east Saturday to eject into Texas by Monday before turning to the northeast. For eastern Utah and Western Colorado, we'll see a ridge building east off the Pacific through the weekend bringing a weak northerly flow aloft keeping skies mostly clear with only high thin clouds. With all the surface moisture available, can't rule out a light afternoon shower on the higher terrain, but no significant accumulations are likely. With the moist ground and clear skies, fog may develop in the valleys overnight into the morning hours as about the only weather phenomenon, burning off by about 9 AM. This ridge develops into a high in the great Basin by about mid next week, but models are diverging by mid week on timing and track of the passing systems. The general consensus is another cut off low passing to the south along the Mexican Border about mid week undercutting the ridge, and a deep trough and low digging south along the West Coast next weekend to push the high/ridge east out onto the Plains. For the most part, we will see mild, dry weather for the coming week with generally light breezes and daytime temperatures running about five degrees above normal. It looks like this week will be a good time to finish getting your yard and things ready for winter, because winter is coming (that's not a forecast, just a fact).

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: The upper ridge starts to flatten across the Rockies on Monday, with slightly more downslope flow leading to better mixing and warmer temperatures in the mid to upper 60s across the plains both Monday and Tuesday, and mainly in the 50s to lower 60s across the higher terrain.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry conditions with at and above seasonal temperatures expected into the middle of next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Current water vapor imagery and upper air analysis has a broad upper trough translating across the Upper Midwest, with an upper low digging across the Desert Southwest into Old Mexico, leaving the Central Rockies in weak west to northwest flow at this time. Regional radars and satellites indicate some passing clouds across the far southeast plains, with precipitation associated with the upper low well south of the region across southern New Mexico at this time.

With expected light winds and decreasing clouds through the rest of the night, we can't rule out some patchy fog developing across the lower Arkansas River valley and portions of the San Luis Valley, with these areas having saturated soils after ample amounts of precipitation over the past few days. Any fog that develops will quickly dissipate after sunrise, leading to a beautiful fall day expected across south central and southeast Colorado on Saturday, under mostly sunny skies. Temperatures to warm slightly over Friday's values, with highs expected to be in the upper 50s to lower 60s across the plains, and mainly in the 40s and 50s across the higher terrain, save for 30s at the peaks. Overnight lows Saturday night to remain at to slightly above seasonal levels in the 20s and 30s areawide, warmest across the plains.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Latest model data continues to support dry weather with temperatures warming back to above seasonal levels through early next week, as upper level ridging builds back across the Great Basin and into the Rockies. With weak flow aloft and at the surface limiting mixing, latest NBM data is a tad lower with highs on Sunday than other guidance may suggest. However, with ample sunshine and light winds, temperatures slightly above seasonal levels in the low 60s will likely feel warmer than the ambient temperature indicates.

The upper ridge starts to flatten across the Rockies on Monday, with slightly more downslope flow leading to better mixing and warmer temperatures in the mid to upper 60s across the plains both Monday and Tuesday, and mainly in the 50s to lower 60s across the higher terrain. A passing wave across the Northern Rockies Tuesday night looks to send a dry front across the plains and leading to slightly cooler, but still around seasonal temperatures on Wednesday. Upper level ridging then looks to rebuild across the Central Rockies through the end of the work week, leading to continued dry conditions along with at and above seasonal temperatures.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Forecast confidence drops substantively after Friday. Ensemble guidance suggests a cooler, wetter trend heading into next weekend, though around 35% of ensemble members still favor higher 500-mb heights and ridging next Saturday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry and increasingly mild weather will persist, with temperatures rising to 5 to 10 degrees above normal by Monday. Isolated areas of fog may develop late tonight in prone areas such as the Cache Valley.
- Model guidance suggests the next precipitation chances hold off until at least next weekend.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Recent satellite imagery shows mostly clear skies across the region, with areas of valley fog quickly dissipating late this morning across portions of the Wasatch Back, Cache Valley, and Upper Sevier River Valleys. Building high pressure will bring stable conditions and a warming, drying trend to the region through at least Monday, with temperatures rising to 5 to 10 degrees above normal.

On Tuesday, a dry shortwave trough will graze across northern Utah, producing a minimal drop in temperatures by a few degrees alongside 700-mb temperatures dropping to around 0C to +2C from around +5C on Monday. This shortwave could also act to mix out any developing valley haze, though it's unclear whether or not the subtle mixing will be enough to fully mix out valleys. Afterwards, high pressure will return with temperatures rising once again through at least the end of the week.

Forecast confidence drops substantively after Friday. Ensemble guidance suggests a cooler, wetter trend heading into next weekend, though around 35% of ensemble members still favor higher 500-mb heights and ridging next Saturday.

2660.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: Generally safe avalanche conditions exist. Lower elevation slopes hold too little snow to produce avalanches, while snow on higher elevation slopes settles and weakens under continued mild weather.
Steer clear of stiff wind-drifted pockets of snow in the alpine, and beware of early-season hazards at lower elevations, such as shallowly buried rocks.

2747.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: Most slopes hold too little snow to produce an avalanche. At high elevations, steer around areas of firm, drifted snow if you find them below ridges or in gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

(Precipitation data are recorded from Secesh SNOTEL site at 6540')

• December - 68" (12.6" SWE)

• February - 41" (5.4" SWE)
• March - 24" (5.2" SWE) Peak Height of Snow - 70" (03/05)

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: Most slopes are generally safe for travel. If you find more than about two feet of snow on the ground or see evidence of recent wind-drifting on a steep slope, consider avoiding that terrain. Stiffer pockets of wind-drifted snow are common, like just below ridgelines and along gully walls. Because wind speeds have been light, the drifted snow may be softer and less obvious than the typical Colorado wind slab. Most slopes near and below treeline hold too little snow to produce an avalanche.
